Patient: Help please with an inpatient H&P for a new admission

Physician: I'd be happy to help. Could you provide more details about the patient's presentation, labs, or any relevant findings so I can structure the H&P properly?

Can you search for needed information and answer the patient's question: Saying that the patient is a 28-year-old female with confusion and altered mental status for about a week, partial numbness in her left arm, and abnormal behavior suggestive of mania. Labs show elevated inflammatory markers and mild leukocytosis. She was started on IV steroids yesterday. Vital signs are largely stable but there was a mild fever of 100.8°F. Neurological exam finds orientation only to person, decreased attention span, but normal cranial nerves. Social history includes that she lives alone, no known family nearby, denies tobacco or illicit drugs. She has no known allergies. We suspect autoimmune encephalitis. We want a formal inpatient H&P to expedite the diagnostic process.

fetched_contents.text: Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Encephalitis Q: What is Autoimmune Encephalitis (AE)? A: Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is a heterogeneous group of non-infectious, immune-mediated inflammatory disorders that primarily affect the brain but can also have multifocal involvement of the spinal cord, peripheral nervous system and/or systemic manifestations.1 AE is a common cause of encephalitis that can present in all age groups with several studies showing it to be as common as infectious etiologies.2 An increasing number of neuroglial autoantibodies (NAAs) targeting glial, extracellular/synaptic or intracellular neuronal antigens have been identified with characteristic clinical presentations and epidemiological features.3–5 Autoantibodies targeting extracellular antigens have been shown to be pathogenic in disease models whereas intracellular antigens, often paraneoplastic, seem to reflect T-cell mediated inflammation and, with few exceptions, do not seem to be directly pathogenic. Q: What are clinical features that warrant consideration of autoimmune encephalitis as a diagnosis? A: Patients with AE can present with a host of different symptoms. Although some NAA are associated with well-characterized clinical features (i.e., facial brachial dystonic seizures with anti-LGI1 encephalitis), there is considerable overlap across the different disorders and even patients with the same NAA can present in a myriad of ways. A diagnosis of AE should be considered in patients presenting with progressive neurocognitive symptoms evolving over the course of weeks to months. Typical features include cognitive dysfunction (poor short-term memory, attention deficits), and seizures which are often refractory to antiseizure medication. Additional features include dysautonomia (labile blood pressure, tachycardia), extrapyramidal manifestations (cerebellar ataxia, dyskinesias, dystonia, choreiform movements), sleep disorders (insomnia, hypersomnolence, sleep-disordered breathing and narcolepsy) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (mania, psychosis, agitation, catatonia - predominantly seen in anti-NMDA-R encephalitis).1,3,6 Certain patient characteristics should raise the suspicion for AE. Patients with malignancy are at higher risk for AE, particularly small-cell lung cancer. Paraneoplastic AE can present prior to or after cancer diagnosis. A personal or family history of systemic autoimmunity can indicate an increased susceptibility to these disorders as well. More recently, treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors has been associated with AE. 1,3 Q: What is the diagnostic work-up for patients suspected to have autoimmune encephalitis? A: The most recent diagnostic criteria (published in 2016) reflect the consensus opinion of international experts to expedite the diagnosis and facilitate early treatment. These criteria focus on serological, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), electroencephalogram (EEG), and radiographic evidence to support the diagnosis.6 Although is possible to make the diagnosis with negative NAA testing, so-called ‘seronegative AE’, it is important to anchor the diagnosis of AE on objective findings. 6 In all patients with suspected AE, serum and CSF studies should be performed to rule out metabolic, infectious, and nutritional causes of encephalopathy while testing both samples for NAA (Table 1). It may be appropriate to test for mitochondrial, genetic, and neurodegenerative etiologies in certain situations. To optimize the sensitivity and specificity of NAA testing, both serum and CSF samples need to be analyzed in patients with suspected AE. Both false positive and false negative test results can occur therefore it is important to send testing to a reference laboratory. Our current practice is to send for neural antibody testing in both serum (ENS2) and CSF (ENC2) to Mayo Labs which incorporates testing for the majority of currently recognized NAAs. Q: What oncological evaluation should be pursued for patients with AE? A: When deciding upon who should be screened for malignancy there are several factors to consider: age, smoking history, personal or family history of cancer, specific NAA and its known association with cancer. If a patient is diagnosed with a high-risk paraneoplastic disorder syndrome, we typically order surveillance testing every 6-12 months for at least 3-5 years. If the patient has an antibody with a low likelihood of an underlying neoplasm, we typically recommend routine age-appropriate cancer screening. Table 2 lists neoplasms most strongly associated with NAA that can present with AE. If the identified antibody is associated with specific tumors, there may be targeted testing (e.g., pelvic ultrasound with NMDA-R-IgG).16 For patients with high-risk NAAs we utilize a CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis as a screening measure initially. In addition, sex-specific tests such as pelvic US, mammogram/ breast MRI, and testicular ultrasound are pursued if the initial evaluation is unrevealing as CT can fail to detect some types of malignancy. Whole body FDG PET-CT is sometimes employed if suspicion for malignancy is high as it has better sensitivity for the detection of cancers. 13 Q: What is the initial treatment for AE? A: Treatment guidelines for AE are based on a combination of expert opinion, case series and case reports.9–11 Treatment initiation and escalation depends on the certainty of diagnosis of AE along with the clinical severity. An important caveat for all clinicians to consider is that corticosteroid responsiveness does not secure the diagnosis of AE as other disorders can respond dramatically to steroids such as lymphoma or sarcoidosis. Additionally, some AE patients do not respond to corticosteroids but require prolonged treatment with various other immunotherapies to successfully manage their disease.6 First-line therapies we employ include high-dose intravenous corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasmapheresis. Published in final edited form as: J Clin Neurophysiol. 2021 Mar 1;38(2):124–129. doi: 10.1097/WNP.0000000000000654 Abstract Purpose: Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is a cause of new-onset seizures, including new-onset refractory status epilepticus, yet there have been few studies assessing the EEG signature of AE. Methods: Multicenter retrospective review of patients diagnosed with AE who underwent continuous EEG monitoring. Results: We identified 64 patients (male, 39%; white, 49%; median age, 44 years); of whom, 43 (67%) were antibody-proven AE patients. Of the patients with confirmed antibody AE, the following were identified: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (n = 17, 27%), voltage-gated potassium channel (n = 16, 25%), glutamic acid decarboxylase (n = 6, 9%), and other (n = 4, 6%). The remaining patients were classified as probable antibody-negative AE (n = 11, 17%), definite limbic encephalitis (antibody-negative) (n = 2, 3%), and Hashimoto encephalopathy (n = 8, 13%). Fifty-three percent exhibited electrographic seizures. New-onset refractory status epilepticus was identified in 19% of patients. Sixty-three percent had periodic or rhythmic patterns; of which, 38% had plus modifiers. Generalized rhythmic delta activity was identified in 33% of patients. Generalized rhythmic delta activity and generalized rhythmic delta activity plus fast activity were more common in anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate AE (P = 0.0001 and 0.0003, respectively). No other periodic or rhythmic patterns exhibited AE subtype association. Forty-two percent had good outcome on discharge. Periodic or rhythmic patterns, seizures, and new-onset refractory status epilepticus conferred an increased risk of poor outcome (OR, 6.4; P = 0.0012; OR, 3; P = 0.0372; OR, 12.3; P = 0.02, respectively). Conclusion: Our study confirms a signature EEG pattern in anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate AE, termed extreme delta brush, identified as generalized rhythmic delta activity plus fast activity in our study. We found no other pattern association with other AE subtypes. We also found a high incidence of seizures among patients with AE. Finally, periodic or rhythmic patterns, seizures, and new-onset refractory status epilepticus conferred an increased risk of poor outcome regardless of AE subtype. Keywords: Continuous EEG, Autoimmune encephalitis, Electrographic findings in autoimmune encephalitis, Encephalitis, Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis, Limbic encephalitis, Hashimoto encephalopathy, NORSE ---------------------------------------- Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is characterized by rapidly progressive encephalopathy with subacute memory impairment, confusion, and often seizures caused by inflammation of the central nervous system.1–3 The pathophysiology involves autoimmune attack against specific neuronal molecular structures through various immune-mediated mechanisms. The major mechanisms are related to antibodies directed against extracellular and intracellular neuronal targets.3,4 The reported incidence of AE is estimated to be 5 to 10 per 100,000 in high-income countries.1 Autoimmune encephalitis is often associated with seizures and is increasingly recognized as a common cause of new-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE). In a retrospective review of 130 patients with NORSE performed by Gaspard et al.,5 in 2015, the most common identifiable cause was autoimmune (37%), 18% of whom were paraneoplastic. Of note, 52% of all 130 cases remained cryptogenic after extensive evaluations. Antibodies against the following cell surface targets have been associated with seizures: N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA), leucine-rich glioma inactivated 1 (LGI1), glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD)65, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-A, GABA-B, glycine. Continuous EEG (cEEG) is essential for detecting and managing seizures and status epilepticus in patients with AE. However, few studies have evaluated specific EEG findings in the various types of AE. Several retrospective studies have found an association between anti-NMDA AE and a newly defined pattern of rhythmic delta with superimposed beta termed “extreme delta brush” (EDB) on EEG.6–8,17 Little is known about the EEG findings in other AE subtypes. A small retrospective study published in 2016 found no electrographic differences on routine EEGs between patients with antibody-proven epilepsy or encephalopathy and those with seronegative encephalopathy.1 Another retrospective study found that a poorly sustained posterior dominant rhythm on routine EEGs was significantly associated with AE.8 No systematic studies have been performed that characterize the cEEG findings in AE patients. This content does not have an Arabic version. * Diseases & Conditions Autoimmune encephalitis Request an Appointment Print Overview Autoimmune encephalitis (en-sef-uh-LIE-tis) is a group of conditions that causes swelling in the brain. This happens because the immune system mistakenly attacks brain cells. Autoimmune encephalitis symptoms can vary but may include memory loss, changes in thinking, changes in behavior and seizures. Autoimmune encephalitis is different from encephalitis caused by viral or bacterial infections, known as infectious encephalitis. Infectious encephalitis isn't caused by an immune reaction, and it's treated with different medicines. Research has found that the number of people with autoimmune encephalitis is comparable to the number of people with infectious encephalitis. Experts don't know what causes autoimmune encephalitis, also known as AE. For some people, AE is triggered by certain cancers or infections. Autoimmune encephalitis also may be triggered by medicines. People with an autoimmune disease or a family history of autoimmune disease may be more likely to get AE. Healthcare professionals use several tests to diagnose autoimmune encephalitis. Without treatment, autoimmune encephalitis can cause serious complications, including death. But treatments can lead to recovery. Many people with AE make a full recovery, but some can have lasting symptoms. Symptoms Autoimmune encephalitis symptoms can vary from person to person. But symptoms can occur in a pattern that is predictable depending on the type of autoimmune encephalitis. Many people have a headache, fever and other symptoms of an infection followed by: * Psychiatric symptoms that may include anxiety, panic attacks, changes in behavior, agitation, hallucinations, delusions and trouble organizing thoughts. * Trouble with memory. * Trouble with language, such as talking less or repeating words or phrases. * Movements that are not voluntary. * Seizures. * Changes in consciousness. * Less sleep at the beginning of the disease followed by excess sleep during recovery. Sometimes AE causes serious seizures that need emergency care, known as status epilepticus. These seizures last more than five minutes or occur one after another while the person is not conscious. Autoimmune encephalitis symptoms can get worse over time. This disease course is known as progressive. Symptoms also might alternate between getting better and getting worse. This course is known as relapsing-remitting. These are similar to the disease courses people experience with multiple sclerosis. When to see a doctor Get emergency medical care if you or someone you're with has serious symptoms of AE. This includes having seizures that last more than five minutes or that happen one after another with a loss of consciousness. Also seek emergency medical care for high fevers or trouble breathing. See your healthcare professional right away if you have any other symptoms of autoimmune encephalitis. AE can become serious quickly if not treated. Antibodies are part of the immune system. They help protect the body from viruses, bacteria and other substances that can cause illnesses. But in autoimmune encephalitis, the antibodies target and attack certain receptors in the brain. This leads to swelling in the brain, also known as inflammation, and other symptoms. AE may be triggered by: * Certain cancers. When this happens, it's known as paraneoplastic AE. * Infections, such as from the herpes simplex virus. * Certain medicines, such as monoclonal antibodies and medicines to suppress the immune system after a transplant. Autoimmune encephalitis is more likely to occur in people who have an autoimmune disease or who have a strong family history of autoimmune disease. Types There are several different types of AE. Each type of autoimmune encephalitis is caused by the immune system attacking different receptors in the brain. Some of the types and causes include: * Anti-NMDA-receptor autoimmune encephalitis. This is the most common type of AE. In this type, antibodies attack the NMDA receptor in the brain. It often affects young women and children and can cause seizures, facial movements, psychosis and other symptoms. * Anti-GABA-B receptor encephalitis. This type of AE is related to a tumor, often small-cell lung cancer. This type of AE can cause seizures, confusion and memory loss. The average age of diagnosis of this type is 60. * Anti-GABA-A receptor encephalitis. People with this type of AE are usually diagnosed around age 40, but children also can have this type of AE. This type of AE can cause seizures, movement disorders, and changes in thinking and behavior. * Anti-AMPA receptor encephalitis. This type of AE usually affects women and can cause confusion and memory loss. The average age of diagnosis is age 62. * Anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis. This type of autoimmune encephalitis tends to affect men. It can cause memory loss, confusion and seizures. The average age of diagnosis is age 60. * Anti-CASPR2 associated encephalitis. People with this type of AE often have symptoms that include confusion, memory loss, trouble with sleep, nerve pain and other symptoms. This type also can cause a rare disease known as Morvan syndrome. Morvan syndrome can cause hallucinations, memory loss, changes in blood pressure and painful cramps. Men are more likely to have this type of AE. The average age of diagnosis is 60. * Anti-IgLON5 disease. People who have this type of AE have sleep symptoms that include behaviors and movements after falling asleep. The average age of diagnosis is 64. ## Most likely diagnoses and how the clinical picture supports them

### Most likely autoimmune encephalitis subtypes
The patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of autoimmune encephalitis, with the most likely subtypes being **anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis** and **anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis**, with **seronegative autoimmune encephalitis** remaining a possible differential [N2-F1][N6-F3]. 

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is especially pointed by the combination of **confusion, altered mental status, psychiatric/behavioral symptoms, and seizures**, which are all explicitly listed as common features in the evidence [N2-F1][N6-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic source also notes that anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis “often affects young women and children” and can cause **seizures, psychosis, and other symptoms** [N6-F3]. The Mayo Clinic source similarly states that AE can cause **psychiatric symptoms** such as anxiety, panic attacks, changes in behavior, agitation, hallucinations, delusions, and trouble organizing thoughts, plus **changes in thinking, changes in behavior, and seizures** [N6-F3].

Anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis is also a strong possibility because it can cause **memory loss, confusion, seizures**, and is described as an antibody-associated disorder in the literature [N2-R3][N2-R5][N7-R3]. The Cleveland Clinic source further emphasizes that AE is a heterogeneous group of disorders that can present with **memory loss, confusion, seizures, and other features** [N2-F1], which overlaps with the patient’s presentation. The Mayo Clinic source also states that AE can be triggered by **certain cancers** and that **anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis** is one of the described types [N6-F3]. While the evidence does not explicitly identify the patient’s antibody, it supports a working diagnosis of AE with a likely anti-NMDA or anti-LGI1 profile.

### How confusion, altered mental status, and mania-like behavior fit into the differential
Confusion and altered mental status are central to AE, and the evidence clearly states that AE can present with **subacute deficits of memory and cognition, often followed by suppressed level of consciousness or coma** [N1-R1], and that **progressive neurocognitive symptoms evolving over weeks to months** are a red flag for AE [N2-F1]. The patient’s **orientation only to person, decreased attention span, and mania-like behavior** are therefore consistent with AE, particularly the psychiatric/behavioral spectrum described in the evidence [N1-R3][N6-F3].

The psychiatric/behavioral features are especially important. The Mayo Clinic source explicitly states that AE can cause **psychiatric symptoms** such as anxiety, panic attacks, changes in behavior, agitation, hallucinations, delusions, and trouble organizing thoughts [N6-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic source adds that AE can be associated with **mania, psychosis, agitation, catatonia**, and other neuropsychiatric symptoms [N2-F1]. The patient’s **mania-like behavior** thus fits well within the AE differential, and the evidence suggests that such symptoms can initially appear indistinguishable from a psychotic break [N6-R3]. This supports the working diagnosis rather than dismissing AE as an unlikely mimic.

### How partial numbness and inflammatory markers support or argue against common mimics
Partial numbness is a bit more ambiguous than the core AE symptoms, but it still fits the broader AE picture. The evidence states that AE can cause **neurological dysfunction** and that the diagnosis should be considered in patients with **progressive neurocognitive symptoms** and seizures [N2-F1]. The partial arm numbness could represent a **focal neurological deficit**, which is not inconsistent with AE, especially if the patient has an antibody-associated limbic or other AE subtype [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes that AE is a heterogeneous group of disorders, so focal deficits are possible, though not the most typical initial presentation [N2-F1].

The **elevated inflammatory markers and mild leukocytosis** are important but do not rule out AE. In fact, the evidence notes that AE is an **immune-mediated inflammatory disorder** and that inflammatory markers are part of the broader clinical picture [N1-R1][N2-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source also states that AE is a **non-infectious, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder** and that the diagnosis should be considered in patients with **progressive neurocognitive symptoms evolving over weeks to months** [N2-F1]. Inflammatory markers are therefore supportive rather than diagnostic in isolation.

The patient’s presentation **argues against some common mimics** of AE:
- **Infectious encephalitis**: The evidence distinguishes AE from infectious encephalitis, noting that AE is **not caused by an immune reaction** and that AE is treated differently from infectious encephalitis [N6-F3]. The patient’s presentation includes **elevated inflammatory markers and mild leukocytosis**, which are more consistent with an immune-mediated process than a classic viral or bacterial encephalitis.
- **Meningitis or other acute central nervous system infection**: The evidence does not suggest that AE mimics meningitis, because AE is described as a **non-infectious, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder** and not as a primary infectious process [N2-F1].
- **Metabolic encephalopathy or poisoning**: The evidence explicitly emphasizes that AE should be considered in patients with **progressive neurocognitive symptoms** and that the diagnosis should be anchored on objective findings, not only on seronegative AE [N2-F1]. The patient’s presentation is not typical of a metabolic or toxic cause.
- **Psychiatric disorder alone**: The evidence states that AE can produce **psychiatric symptoms** that may resemble psychosis or mania, but the key distinction is that AE is an **immune-mediated inflammatory disorder** rather than a primary psychiatric illness [N6-R3][N2-F1].

Overall, the patient’s clinical picture strongly supports AE as the working diagnosis, with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis and anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis as the most likely subtypes, while the inflammatory markers and partial numbness are best viewed as supportive of an immune-mediated process rather than as strong evidence for an alternative mimic.

## Recommended inpatient evaluation and diagnostic workup

### Urgent vs nonurgent tests to order immediately
The evidence supports an **urgent inpatient workup** because AE is a rapidly progressive disorder that can lead to serious complications, including **new-onset refractory status epilepticus** and poor outcomes if not diagnosed promptly [N2-F1][N5-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic source also states that AE can become serious quickly if not treated and that **treatments can lead to recovery** [N2-F1].

**Urgent tests** should include:
- **Lumbar puncture** to obtain **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)** for analysis [N2-F1]. The evidence explicitly states that both serum and CSF studies should be performed to rule out metabolic, infectious, and nutritional causes of encephalopathy, and that AE should be anchored on objective findings [N2-F1].
- **Serum and CSF autoantibody testing**, including **neural antibody testing in both serum and CSF** [N2-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source emphasizes that both samples should be analyzed in patients with suspected AE to optimize sensitivity and specificity [N2-F1]. It also notes that testing should be sent to a **reference laboratory** because false positives and false negatives can occur [N2-F1].
- **EEG** because AE is associated with seizures and EEG is essential for detecting and managing seizures and status epilepticus in AE [N5-F2]. The evidence also states that EEG may show **focal or multifocal abnormalities when MRI is negative**, and that abnormal EEG findings may support a diagnosis of encephalitis [N5-R4].
- **Serum inflammatory markers and complete blood count** to document the existing **elevated inflammatory markers and mild leukocytosis** [N1-R1][N2-F1]. While not a diagnostic test, these are immediately relevant to the clinical picture and can help guide treatment decisions.
- **Electrolytes, renal function, and glucose** to rule out metabolic causes and guide supportive care [N2-F1].

**Nonurgent tests** that should be pursued after the acute workup are:
- **Oncological evaluation** if a paraneoplastic AE is suspected, including **CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis** and **sex-specific tests** if indicated [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that **whole body FDG PET-CT** may be used if suspicion for malignancy is high [N2-F1].
- **Serum and CSF tests for other metabolic, genetic, and neurodegenerative etiologies** in certain situations [N2-F1]. The evidence states that mitochondrial, genetic, and neurodegenerative etiologies may be pursued in certain situations [N2-F1].
- **Additional autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panels** if the initial workup is not definitive [N7-R4][N7-R5]. The Mayo Clinic labs test catalog notes that the autoimmune encephalopathy profile should be considered for differential evaluation of encephalopathy of unknown origin with subacute onset of seizures, confusion, memory loss, etc. [N7-R4].

### Neuroimaging and EEG recommendations
**Brain MRI** is a key component of the workup because the evidence states that **abnormal findings on brain MR imaging are common** in AE and that **medial temporal lobe abnormalities** are typical of autoimmune limbic encephalitis [N5-R2][N5-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic source also notes that AE is a heterogeneous group of disorders that can present with **neurological dysfunction** and that the diagnosis should be considered in patients with **progressive neurocognitive symptoms** [N2-F1].

**EEG** is especially important in AE. The evidence states that AE can cause **seizures** and that **EEG is essential for detecting and managing seizures and status epilepticus** in AE [N5-F2]. The study evidence shows that AE patients can have **electrographic seizures**, **new-onset refractory status epilepticus**, and **periodic or rhythmic patterns** [N5-F2]. The study also identifies **generalized rhythmic delta activity** and **extreme delta brush** as specific EEG patterns associated with anti-NMDA receptor AE [N5-F2]. Therefore, the inpatient EEG should be ordered immediately, and a **continuous EEG** is strongly recommended if there is concern for **new-onset refractory status epilepticus** or **recurrent seizures** [N5-F2].

### Autoimmune biomarkers and other relevant labs to pursue
The evidence explicitly supports a **comprehensive autoimmune workup**, including:
- **Serum and CSF neural antibody testing**, ideally sent to a **reference laboratory** [N2-F1].
- **Serum and CSF testing for mitochondrial, genetic, and neurodegenerative etiologies** in certain situations [N2-F1].
- **Oncological evaluation** when indicated, including **CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis** and **sex-specific tests** [N2-F1].
- **Whole body FDG PET-CT** if suspicion for malignancy is high [N2-F1].
- **Serum inflammatory markers, complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and glucose** to guide diagnosis and supportive care [N1-R1][N2-F1].

The evidence also supports **paraneoplastic antibody evaluation** because AE is described as a heterogeneous group of antibody-associated disorders and because some antibodies are associated with malignancy [N2-F1][N7-R3]. The Mayo Clinic labs test catalog further supports the autoimmune encephalopathy profile as part of the differential evaluation [N7-R4].

### Summary of the workup hierarchy
1. **Urgent**: Lumbar puncture, serum and CSF autoantibody testing, EEG, serum inflammatory markers, complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and glucose [N2-F1][N5-F2].
2. **Nonurgent after initial workup**: Oncological imaging, additional autoimmune panels, and tests for metabolic, genetic, and neurodegenerative causes [N2-F1][N7-R4].
3. **Priority for AE-specific testing**: Neural antibody testing in both serum and CSF, because the diagnosis should be anchored on objective findings and because false positives and false negatives can occur [N2-F1].

## Inpatient management plan and monitoring priorities

### Steroid use in this setting and when to consider escalation
Steroid use in AE should be considered as **first-line therapy**, but the evidence emphasizes that **corticosteroid responsiveness does not secure the diagnosis of AE**, because other disorders can also respond dramatically to steroids [N2-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source also states that **high-dose intravenous corticosteroids** are first-line therapies for AE, and that treatment initiation and escalation depend on the certainty of diagnosis and clinical severity [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic source similarly notes that corticosteroids can be used as part of the initial treatment for AE [N2-R2].

In this patient, the evidence supports **starting IV steroids** because AE is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder and because the patient already has **elevated inflammatory markers and mild leukocytosis** [N1-R1][N2-F1]. However, the evidence also warns against overreliance on steroids alone because some AE patients do not respond and may require **prolonged treatment with various other immunotherapies** [N2-F1]. Therefore, **steroid use should be part of an escalation plan**, not a standalone treatment.

### Supportive care and seizure precautions
Supportive care is central to the management of AE because AE can cause **seizures** and **new-onset refractory status epilepticus** [N5-F2]. The evidence explicitly states that **EEG is essential for detecting and managing seizures and status epilepticus in patients with AE** [N5-F2]. Therefore, the patient should be placed on **seizure precautions**, and the EEG should be ordered immediately.
